titleStmt.title: Probabilistic Response Time Analysis for Fixed Preemption Point Selection

analytic.title: Probabilistic Response Time Analysis for Fixed Preemption Point Selection

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Preemption point selection has a significant impact on the schedulability of Real-Time tasks under the Fixed Preemption Point approach in Limited Preemptive Scheduling. Many real time systems can occasionally tolerate deadline misses as long as their occurrence does not exceed a specified probabilistic threshold. However, the existing approaches for preemption point selection are inappropriate for such systems, as they are mainly aiming to provide hard guarantees, considering worst case (upper bounded) preemption overheads. Additionally, the worst case preemption overheads typically occur with very low probabilities. In this paper, we propose a novel preemption point selection approach, and an associated probabilistic response time analysis, considering preemption related overheads modelled as probabilistic distributions. The method is suitable for providing solutions in systems that can occasionally tolerate deadline misses. Our method is able to find solutions, in terms of preemption point selections, in all cases where the existing approaches do. Moreover, it provides preemption point selections for additional tasksets that guarantees the overall taskset schedulability with a certain probability. The evaluation results show an improvement with respect to increasing the number of tasksets for which a preemption point selection is possible compared to existing, upper-bound based, selection approaches. The results show that the deadline miss probabilities of the tasksets and associated preemption point selections are considerably low.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: During the past decades, the real-time non-preemptive scheduling and fully preemptive scheduling have been extensively investigated as well as compared with each other. It has been shown that none of the two scheduling paradigms dominates over the other in terms of schedulability, e.g., nonpreemptive scheduling introduces the cost of blocking by lower priority tasks, while fully preemptive scheduling comes with a cost of preemption related overheads. Limited Preemptive Scheduling (LPS) has emerged as an attractive alternative with respect to, e.g., increasing real-time systems schedulability, efficiently reducing the blocking by lower priority tasks (compared to non-preemptive scheduling) and efficiently controlling the number of preemptions, thus controlling the overall preemption related overhead of the system.

There are three main LPS approaches that enable reducing the overall preemption related overhead, e.g., Preemption Thresholds Scheduling (LP-PTS) proposed by Wang and Saksena [1], Deferred Preemption Scheduling (LP-DPS) proposed by Baruah [2] and Fixed Preemption Points (LP-FPP), proposed by Burns [3]. LP-FPP offers the advantage of predictability with respect to the preemption related overhead compared to the PTS and DPS [4]. The main reason is that the preemption points of a task in LP-FPP are explicitly defined by the programmers during the design phase, unlike the LP-PTS and LP-DPS approaches where the preemption points are not known in advance, thus, in this paper we address LP-FPP.

Preemption related overhead is acknowledged to be a significant cost that influences schedulability in modern systems and it has received a great attention during the past decades [5], [4]. It has been shown that preemptions can introduce significant runtime overhead which may lead to high variations in the execution time of the tasks, that in turn may increase the worst case execution time of a task by as much as 33% [6]. Preemption related overheads are mainly composed of several types of hardware related costs, e.g., scheduling cost, pipeline cost, bus-related cost etc. However, the cache-related preemption delay (CRPD) is often the largest part of the preemption related overhead. Moreover, CRPD is often characterised with a high variance during the runtime as it heavily depends on the specific preemption point in the code of a preempted task and the evicting scenarios caused by the preempting tasks, as shown by Altmeyer et al. [7], Gebhard et al. [8] and Li et al. [9], and further confirmed by Bastoni et al. [5] who provided empirical results about CRPDs from simulations on real hardware. They also showed the empirical measurements with statistical observations pointing that the average CRPDs are significantly low compared to the upper-bound CRPD values (ratio of 1 : 100 respectively). In a recent work, Davis et al. [10] proposed the analysis of probabilistic cache related preemption delays. Hence, an appropriate preemption point selection, to positively affect the overall schedulability, needs to take into account the probabilistic information about CRPD.

The preemption point selection typically consists of two main steps: 1) selection of preemption points from a set of potential preemption points, followed by 2) schedulability analysis, based on the chosen selection. Bertogna et al. [11] proposed a preemption point selection approach considering upper-bounded overheads, with the goal of maximising the overall taskset schedulability through minimising the cumulative preemption related overheads. However, in many critical real-time systems the guarantees are defined as probability thresholds such that the probability of a system failing to meet its timing constraint should be below this predefined acceptable value [12], [13]. In this context, the existing approaches for preemption point selection, based on upper bound values on the preemption overheads [11], [14], are not fully suitable as they will introduce a significant amount of pessimism in the associated schedulability analysis.

Hence, there is a need to enhance the existing preemption point selection approaches and the associated schedulability analysis by introducing probabilistic models. In particular, we propose a novel probabilistic response time analysis for the evaluation of the impact of preemption related overheads on the schedulability of a system. Building on our previous work [15], we also propose a preemption point selection algorithm that heuristically reduces the deadline miss probability in the system by selecting preemption points that are more likely to decrease the deadline miss probability, which is evaluated by the proposed probabilistic response time analysis.

The evaluation results show that the gain when addressing the preemption point selection for the real time systems with probabilistic constraints is considerable even when we take into account the probability distributions of the preemption related overheads that represent worst case preemption scenarios. During the evaluation we also computed the maximum deadline miss probabilities of the tasksets applying the proposed preemption point selections, which furthermore shows that the proposed selection method may significantly reduce the deadline miss probability of a task system, compared to the naive selection strategies that reduce blocking without considering probabilistic distributions of the overheads.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows: In Section II we describe the preliminaries of the paper such as probabilistic random variable and operations used in the proposed analysis. In Section III we introduce the system model within two subsections: III-A that describes the task model and III-B which describes the probabilistic model extension. In section IV we define the probabilistic response time analysis dividing it into three subsections for each step of the analysis. In section V we describe the preemption point selection algorithm. In Section VI we discuss the evaluation of the approach and in Section VII we conclude the paper.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The system model used in this paper is described in two subsections. First, we describe the task model and its elements considering the worst case timing parameters. In the second part we describe the probabilistic parameters and the relation between the scalar and probabilistic parameters.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: In this paper we consider a real-time sporadic task model Γ which is composed of n tasks τ i (1 ≤ i ≤ n) under uni-processor Fixed Priority (FP) paradigm, ordered in a decreasing priority order. Each task τ i generates an infinite number of task instances τ i,j and is described with a tuple of the following parameters {P i , C i , D i , T i } where P i denotes the task's priority, C i denotes its worst case execution time (WCET), D i denotes a relative deadline (relative to the release time of τ i,j ), and T i denotes the minimum inter-arrival time between two consecutive instances of τ i . Furthermore, in this work we consider the task-splitting model where each task consists of a sequence of m subjobs δ i,k (1 ≤ k ≤ m), with worst case execution times c i,k such that m k=1 c i,k = C i . Consequently, subjobs are separated by m -1 possible preemption points P P i,k which upon preemption introduce the preemption related overhead that may extend the execution time of the succeeding subjob. Therefore, for each subjob δ i,k we also consider the worst case execution time c p i,k including the preemption overhead at preemption point P P i,k-1 . At the beginning of each task we introduce the virtual point P P i,0 .

In Fixed Preemption Point Scheduling, we consider two types of preemption points -possible preemption points PP and selected preemption points SPP. This is the case because the selection of preemption points must be performed before the runtime execution of the task system. A selection for a single task τ i defines a set (SPP i ) of preemption points that are enabled for the runtime preemption. The interval between two consecutive selected preemption points of a same task forms a non-preemptive chunk (NPR).

In Figure 1 we show a task consisting of three subjobs (δ i,1 , δ i,2 and δ i,3 ) separated by two potential preemption points (PP i,1 and PP i,2 ). Since that PP i,2 is the selected preemption point, we differentiate two non-preemptive regions. Also, we account for the preemption overhead at PP i,2 including it in the worst case execution time c p i,3 of the succeeding subjob δ i,3 . We do not include the preemption overhead of PP i,1 to the WCET of the second subjob since PP i,1 is not selected.

div.head: B. Probabilistic Model
div.p: In order to model probabilistic task parameters we distinguish between the two different mathematical terms: 1) probabilistic execution time (pET), and 2) probabilistic WCET (pWCET). Random variables that describe pET are not independent as they depict the actual probabilistic behaviour in the system where the independence among the execution times does not hold. However, pWCET is defined as the random variable obtained as the upper bound on pET, using probabilistic static code analysis, EVT theory, etc., as shown by Cucu-Grosjean [17]. By defining pWCET as the upper bound on pET we estimate random variables such that one pWCET does not affect the other, i.e. Definition II.1 holds. Therefore, for each pET variable used in the paper we define a safe pWCET:
Definition III.1. The probabilistic execution time (E i,j,k ) of a subjob1 δ i,k , of a job τ i,j , describes the probability that the execution time of a subjob in τ i,j is equal to a given value.
Definition III.2. The probabilistic WCET (C i,k ) of a subjob δ i,k , of a task τ i , describes the probability that the WCET of a subjob in τ i is equal to a given value.

Safe probabilistic WCET: The probabilistic WCET C i,k is safe if and only if it is an upper bound of E i,j,k , for all j. Formally, C i,k is safe if and only if ∀j, C i,k E i,j,k . Informally, it means that the CDF of C i,k stays below the CDF of E i,j,k for each value of E i,j,k (for a detailed explanation refer to [17]). Including the preemption effect to the subjob's execution time we also define the following probabilistic variables and the safe upper bound.

Definition III.3. The probabilistic execution time (E p i,j,k ), including a preemption effect at P P i,k-1 , of a subjob δ i,k of a job τ i,j , describes the probability that the execution time of this subjob including a preemption is equal to a given value.

Definition III.4. The probabilistic WCET (C p i,k ) including a preemption effect at P P i,k-1 of a subjob δ i,k , of a task τ i , describes the probability that the WCET of a subjob in τ i including a preemption effect is equal to a given value.

Safe probabilistic WCET including preemption effect: The probabilistic WCET C p i,k is safe if and only if it is an upper bound of E p i,j,k , for all j. Formally, C p i,k is safe if and only if ∀j, C p i,k E p i,j,k . The related work about the probabilistic preemption overhead analysis is proposed by Davis et al. [10]. In that work, the resulting random variable is safe and can be derived for the set of instructions, accounting for the preemption effect at the specified preemption point that precedes the instruction set. Thus, it can be easily integrated with the random variable C p i,k proposed in this paper, with minor changes that would consider the non-preemptive regions (nonpreemptive set of instructions). The probabilistic variables defined in [10] consider the random cache replacement policy. The probabilistic preemption effect on WCET of a subjob can be obtained by various methods, e.g. empirical measurements, simulations, CRPD static code analysis, etc. However, the obtained distributions must be safe, as defined above, in order to be used in the proposed analysis.

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY ANALYSIS
div.p: Schedulability analysis for the given task model is defined by the probabilistic response time analysis that considers the proposed discrete random variables. Hence, the outcome of the response time analysis of a given task job τ i,j is a probabilistic distribution of its different response times. The following analysis relies on the feasibility analysis for the task splitting model proposed by Yao et al. [14] and the probabilistic response time analysis for the task models with probabilistic execution times, proposed by Diaz et al. [18]. However, in this analysis we also consider the defined probabilistic worst case preemption effects on the execution time of the subjobs.

Considering a job τ i,j in the proposed task model and assuming a set of selected preemption points SPP i for each task, there are two distinct execution intervals for which we conduct different computations in order to finally compute the probabilistic response time R i,j . The first execution interval [r i,j , S i,j ] is defined from the release time r i,j of τ i,j until the latest start time of the last non-preemptive chunk, S i,j . Before this interval there is a possibility of blocking B i,j by lower priority jobs or an accumulated pending workload by higher or equal priority jobs started before r i,j . Furthermore, during the execution interval [r i,j , S i,j ] there is a possibility of interference from higher priority jobs. However, after the [r i,j , S i,j ] interval, job τ i,j cannot be preempted or interfered anymore during the execution interval of the last non-preemptive chunk, thus the WCET response time R i,j is equal to the sum of S i,j and the WCET of the last non-preemptive chunk.

Consequently, probabilistic response time analysis of a job τ i,j for the proposed task model starts with the computation of a discrete random variable S i,j i.e. the latest start times of the last NPR of τ i,j . For computing S i,j we consider three significant probabilistic computations (described in detail in Sections IV-A-IV-C) in the following order: A) Computation of the pending workload W (i,ri,j ) at release time r i,j of job τ i,j . B) Computation of the probabilistic execution time of the preemptable interval C i i.e. of the non-preemptive chunks that precede the last non-preemptive chunk. C) Computation of the interference caused by the higher priority jobs, arriving after r i,j , that can preempt job τ i,j or interfere with its latest start time during the execution interval [r i,j , S i,j ]. After S i,j , τ i,j cannot be preempted. Therefore, the general concept (Figure 2) for computing the start time distribution S i,j of the last non-preemptive chunk of τ i,j is:
div.formula: S i,j = W (i,ri,j ) ⊗ C i ⊗ I i,j(3)
div.p: where I i,j is an interference from the higher priority jobs.

Interference is computed iteratively because the interferable interval is enlarged by each single accounted interference from a higher priority job. (more details in Section IV-C). Finally, by convoluting the probabilistic WCET of the last non-preemptive chunk L i we get the probabilistic response time R i,j :
div.formula: R i,j = S i,j ⊗ L i(4)

After τ i,j , the self pushing phenomenon is not possible for the next task intance and its deadline miss probability cannot be larger than the one obtained until τ i,j . Finally, we define the maximum deadline miss probability DMP max of a taskset Γ as the maximum DMP max i in Γ.

div.head: V. PREEMPTION POINT SELECTION ALGORITHM
div.p: In this section we propose a novel preemption point selection algorithm, based on our previous work [15], that aims to minimise the deadline miss probability of a taskset by selecting preemption points that are likely to result in a low deadline miss probability DMP of a given taskset. In order to reduce the over provisioning of the upper bound based selection method, we propose a preemption point selection algorithm based on quantile functions of the probabilistic worst case execution times of subjobs (C i,k and C p i,k ). Therefore, we first define a quantile of the subjob's probabilistic WCET including preemption effect, C p i,k , using the quantile function Q. The quantile function Q(x, C p i,k ) for a given probability x derives the lowest execution time value from the discrete random variable C p i,k such that the probability of the WCET being less or equal to that value is greater or equal to the given probability x. Since we assume that the WCET value c p i,k is always included in C p i,k , consequently the quantile Q(1, C p i,k ) = c p i,k . E.g., To intuitively describe the benefit of using quantile functions for the preemption point selection let us assume that in some task we have only two possible preemption points PP i,1 and PP i,2 with the possible preemption effects on probabilistic worst case execution times of succeeding subjobs: Considering the upper-bound preemption point selection, the affinity of selecting PP i,2 is stronger because its WCET including preemption effect is 80 compared to 100 which is the WCET including preemption effect of PP i,1 . However, let us assume that the selection of any of the two points will definitely cause infeasibility, and now the goal is to reduce the probabilistic impact of the selected point on the deadline miss probability. It is clear from the random variables that the first point causes higher WCET values (40 and 100) but with low probabilities (0.07 and 0.03 respectively) compared to the second point (0.3 and 0.2). By computing the 0.8 quantile of probabilistic WCET, including preemption effect, by both points, the affinity of selecting the first point PP i,1 will be higher compared to selecting PP i,2 because Q(0.8, C p i,1 ) = 10 compared to the Q(0.8, C p i,2 ) = 40 i.e. the probability that the preemption at PP i,1 will cause the WCET value equal to 10 is 0.8, which is also the probability that the preemption at PP i,1 will cause the WCET value that is less or equal to 40. Using the quantile function we can compare the likelihood that the worst case preemption effect from different points will cause certain WCET values, therefore we use this information for the appropriate probabilistic selection. We focus on two variables throughout each iteration of the algorithm (see Algorithm 3): 1. a set SPP of selected points per taskset which produces the lowest deadline miss probability and 2. the resulting deadline miss probability DMP . They are initially set to values infeasible and 1 respectively and updated in each iteration when a selection that causes a smaller deadline miss probability is found. Lines 5-11 in the algorithm are based on the upper-bound based algorithm proposed by Bertogna et al. [11] and will be explained later. For now, it is important to know that this part first computes the quantiles PE x i,k = Q(x, C p i,k ) under a given probability (i.e. confidence level) x for all the probabilistic worst case execution times of subjobs considering preemption effect (line 6) and at the end it returns the selection SPP x computed with respect to the given quantiles (line 13). If the selection cannot be found SPP x is set to infeasible.

div.p: After the computation of quantiles for all the probabilistic worst case execution times of subjobs considering preemption effect, in the first iteration we set the given confidence level x to 1 and the algorithm computes the same selection (line 13) as the upper-bound algorithm proposed by Bertogna et al. The unsuccessful selection will result to infeasible, thus, in the next iteration, we decrease the confidence level by the predefined amount (line 22). In each iteration if the selection SPP p for the updated confidence level is found (line 14), we compute DMP x of the taskset with a selection SPP x (line 15). Next, we check if the computed deadline miss probability DMP x is less than the minimum deadline miss probability DMP computed until the current iteration (line 17). If the selection found in this iteration has a lower DMP than those found previously, we update SPP and DMP (lines [17][18][19][20]. This is repeated until we reach the predefined threshold of the confidence level (e.g., 0.1). When the threshold is reached the algorithm returns the selection SPP producing lowest DMP.

Regarding the part of the algorithm that refers to the task level selection of the preemption points (lines [5][6][7][8][9][10][11], it computes preemption point selections for each task in the taskset in a decreasing priority order, starting from the second task in Γ. First, it computes the quantiles for each subjob considering probabilistic WCET with preemption (line 6) for a task under analysis (e.g.,τ 2 ). Then it computes the maximum blocking tolerances of the higher priority tasks (line 7) as those are the ones whose feasibility can be affected if there exists the nonpreemptive region of the lower priority tasks that is larger than their maximum blocking tolerance. For the selection, we find minimum β i of all of the higher priority blocking tolerances. Next, it computes the optimal preemption point selection (line 9) with respect to β i (for more information refer to [11]). In the next step (line 10), the algorithm updates the execution time of the task by adding the derived quantiles of the now selected points to the non-preemptive worst case execution time of a task. These steps are repeated until we compute preemption point selection for τ n . Finally, upon reaching the τ n it is important to check the feasibility of this task (line 12), because it also can be affected by the execution time updates computed in order to address the added preemption effects from the selected points of the higher priority tasks and τ n itself. If this final condition is met then we have a feasible preemption point selection SPP x computed by uniting the preemption point selections of each task in a taskset (line 13).

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: We conducted a number of experiments in order to investigate the applicability of the proposed selection algorithm. The purpose of the experiments was to investigate the impact of the proposed preemption point selection, considering a probabilistic model of preemption related overheads, on a deadline miss probability of the task sets deemed infeasible by the upper-bound based selections.

In the experiment setup we generate 2000 synthetic tasksets consisting of 7 to 19 tasks, respectively (depending on the experiment). In order to generate WCET values for each task, we used the established experimental setup for LP-FPP task sets based on real runtime tasks, proposed by Bertogna et al. [11]. Thus, each task consists of random number of subjobs generated in the range [20,200] and the WCET of each subjob (wes) is generated from the normal Gaussian distribution with the mean µ = 4000 and the standard deviation δ = 3000. As the main focus of the experiment is on proposed preemption point selection, and therefore on the preemption effects at different preemption points, the probabilistic WCET of a subjob is consistently generated from the normal Gaussian distribution with (µ = 2/3 * wes) and (δ = 1/3 * wes). For each preemption point, the upper bound (po) of the preemption related overhead is generated by the distribution equation proposed by Bertogna et al. [11]. The probabilistic preemption effects for each subjob are generated according to the empirical results proposed by Bastoni et al. [5], but only from the subset of experiments considering the worst case preemption overhead measurements forced by the experiment setup. Therefore, for each subjob's probabilistic WCET, including preemption effect, discrete random variables are generated from Gaussian distributions with randomly generated mean in range µ = [0.18 * po +wes, 0.29 * po +wes] and standard deviation in range δ = [0.1 * po, 0.13 * po]. The size of random variables was set to 20 values. We generated variants of these 2000 tasksets for utilisation ranging from 0.81 to 0,99 by deriving task periods with the U-unifast algorithm [20].

For each taskset we first applied the traditional selection based on upper bounds (UB) proposed by Bertogna et al. [11] with the blocking computation improvement proposed by Yao et al. [14] and then our new method ( = 0.1, quantile threshold = 0.1) taking advantage of the probabilistic model. To investigate the maximum deadline miss probabilities per taskset, we apply our method several times with different maximum deadline miss probability thresholds, meaning that a selection must result in a maximum deadline miss probability lower than the threshold in order to be accepted.

The result of the first experiment, with tasksets consisting of 7 tasks, is shown in Figure 8. As expected, at low utilizations, in most cases a feasible selection can be found using the upper bound method, and our method does not provide significant advantage with respect to the number of additionally facilitated tasksets. However, the majority of the additional selections found affect the maximum deadline miss probabilities of the tasksets below 0.01 threshold, especially in the range of utilizations from 0.81 to 0.97. For example, at utilization 0.87 the upper bound method found selections for 1705 of 2000 tasksets. In addition to these, our method found selections for another 152 tasksets below the 0.01 threshold, and 152 and 154 for thresholds 0.1 and 1. At higher utilizations, where for many tasksets the UB method is unable to find a selection that guarantees schedulability, our method is still able to find selections with very low maximum deadline miss probabilities. For example, at utilization 0.95 the upper bound method found selections for 710 of 2000 tasksets. In addition to these, our method found selections for another 426 tasksets below the 0.01 threshold, and 482 and 546 for thresholds 0.1 and 1.

Next, in order to evaluate the deadline miss probabilities of the tasksets, for which our method is able to find selections but the UB method does not, we generated a number of tasksets until we reach 2000 of those where UB fails to provide a selection (Figure 9). We compared the deadline miss probabilites of tasksets, given the selections from the proposed algorithm (PS) and those given by the naive selection algorithm that selects all possible preemption points for the lower priority tasks than the task whose blocking tolerance is too small for the appropriate upper bound selection. This is the simple selection strategy that aims to reduce the blocking caused by the lower priority tasks. The results show that the proposed selection algorithm succeeds in decreasing the DMP of a taskset to the considerable extents, e.g., at utilization level 0.99, the average DMP of tasksets using naive selection is 0.988, while the proposed algorithm provides DMP of 0.25. Finally, in order to investigate the scalability of the methods as the number of tasks increases, we varied the number of tasks in each generated taskset from 7 to 19, with the fixed utilization of 0.95. We show the resulting ratio between additional selections found by our method and the number of selections found by UB method in Figure 10 (left). In Figure 10, on the right, we show the average deadline miss probabilities of tasksets considering applied selections. As expected, by increasing the number of tasks in the taskset, the ratio of additional selections is decreasing. In the conducted experiment, for the taskset size 7 our method found 43% more selections compared to the number of UB selections, for the taskset size 13 the percentage is 35% and for the taskset size 19 the percentage is 30%. This is the case because the overall preemption related delay impact is higher for the tasksets with smaller number of tasks as those tasks present more selection possibilities and this amplifies the effect of our selection algorithm as well as the UB algorithm. Also, compared to the naive selection, the proposed algorithm scales much better with respect to decreasing the deadline miss probabilities of the tasksets with the assigned selection.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: Considering the impact of preemption related overheads on the task system's schedulability, and also the variability among the possible preemption overhead values, where the WCET occurs rarely, we proposed a novel probabilistic response time analysis for evaluating the impact of preemptions on schedulability of the system. Moreover, the analysis is used by an associated preemption point selection method tailored for providing solutions in systems that can occasionally tolerate deadline misses. For such real time systems, the selection algorithm significantly enlarges the selection possibilities compared to the upper bound based algorithms, therefore enabling the preemption point selections and their evaluation. The proposed algorithm successfully finds a feasible preemption point selection in all cases where the upper bound based method does. Moreover, it provides selections for additional tasksets that guarantees the overall taskset schedulability with a certain probability. Our selection method exploits the information about probabilistic preemption related overhead distributions to select preemption points while aiming to minimise the worst case deadline miss probability. The evaluation results demonstrate the applicability of the approach, especially for systems with high utilisation where our algorithm succeeds in finding solutions for a significant number of additional tasksets, and furthermore provides considerably lower deadline miss probabilities compared to a naive selection approach.
